title: Five arrows north
hookLine: tradition says the Guru sent Banda north with five arrows and five Sikhs

lines: FIVE ARROWS FROM THE GURU'S QUIVER.
FIVE SIKHS, A DRUM, A BANNER.
cards: Five arrows. Not a sword, not a crown, not a treasury. Tradition says that when Guru Gobind Singh sent Banda Singh away from Nanded, toward a Punjab he barely knew, those arrows from the Guru's own quiver went with him.
So did five Sikhs to ride beside him, a drum, a banner, and letters from the Guru telling the Sikhs of Punjab to stand with this man. A long road north, and a stranger at the front of it.

teach.h: ARROWS AS A SEAL, NOT A WEAPON.
teach.b: Why hand a man arrows instead of an army? Sikh tradition reads them as something closer to a seal than a weapon. Five arrows can't win a war.
What they could do was say, to anyone who saw them: the Guru sent me. In Punjab, Banda Singh was unknown.
He had spent his life as a holy man in other places, and the Sikhs there had every reason to ask why they should follow him.
So he carried signs they would recognize: the arrows, the companions, the Guru's letters. Then there's the number. Five keeps turning up in the Sikh story.
Five beloved ones stood up at the first amrit. Five Sikhs ride north here.

teach.h: FIVE: THE MISSION BELONGS TO THE KHALSA.
teach.b: Tradition doesn't explain every five, and it doesn't need to; some readers take the pattern to say this mission belongs to the Khalsa, not to one man. That fits what the tellings say came with the arrows: instructions.
Tradition says the Guru told Banda Singh to keep to truth and a disciplined life, never to set himself up as a Guru, and to remember that he served the Khalsa.
Authority was given, and a limit was given in the same breath.
Some readers find a habit worth keeping here. When you're trusted with a task, you're trusted with two things: the job, and the reminder of whose job it really is. Banda Singh set out with both.
Tomorrow, the road reaches a hard town.

how: Sikhs tell how Guru Gobind Singh sent Banda Singh to Punjab with five arrows, five Sikhs and letters to the sangats, and remember the instructions tradition says came with them.

o: an arrow, one of five sent north as a sign
a drum beaten to call the Sikhs together
a banner carried at the front of the march

games.q: what went north — tap the pairs.

games.q: you're a stranger arriving in a land where nobody knows you, asking people to risk everything with you. what do you bring?
o: a large army of your own.
signs and letters from someone they trust.
a speech about your past powers.
games.why: tradition says Banda Singh carried the Guru's arrows and letters, and came with five Sikhs.

practice: Bring to mind something you've been sent to do, by someone else or by your own conscience, and name it in a few plain words. Then ask slowly: who trusted me with this, and what's the limit, the thing I mustn't do while I do it?
Hold both answers like a few arrows in your hand, and if you pray, say Waheguru on each breath out.

wordCard.voice: Teer, an arrow. One of the five from Guru Gobind Singh's own quiver that, tradition says, Banda Singh carried north to Punjab as a sign the Guru had sent him.

carryVoice: Your line: five arrows. The job and its limit came together, in one hand. See you tomorrow.
